prompt: Why can't you write ordinary unit tests for an LLM feature?
answer_markdown: Unit tests assert that a function returns exactly the expected value, but LLM outputs legitimately vary in wording while remaining equally correct. 'Refunds take up to 14 days' and 'You'll get your money back within two weeks' are both right and share almost no tokens, so an exact-match assertion fails on a correct answer. Tests like these fail intermittently, get marked flaky, and are deleted or skipped within weeks — leaving no coverage at all. The replacement is a fixed dataset of representative inputs scored on quality dimensions, where you compare aggregate scores between versions rather than checking individual outputs for exact equality. Note the important exception: wherever the output is genuinely constrained — a classification label, a JSON schema, a required field, a resolvable citation — ordinary deterministic assertions work perfectly and you should use them, because a surprising amount of LLM quality is checkable that way.

prompt: What is a golden dataset and how would you build one for a support-ticket classifier?
answer_markdown: A golden dataset is a fixed set of inputs with known-good expected outputs or grading criteria, run against every meaningful change so you can compare versions on identical cases. Build it from three sources. First, real production traffic sampled to reflect the actual distribution of ticket types, so your scores mean something about real usage rather than about cases you imagined. Second, every bug you have fixed — each production failure becomes a permanent regression case, which is what stops the same problem recurring. Third, deliberate edge cases: empty input, extremely long input, ambiguous tickets that could plausibly be two categories, out-of-scope requests, and adversarial inputs attempting prompt injection. Fifty well-chosen cases beat five thousand random ones, because coverage of failure modes matters more than volume. The hard part is maintenance rather than creation — as prompts, models, and user behaviour change, a set built once slowly stops representing reality, so it needs periodic refreshing from current traffic.

prompt: You want to use an LLM to grade your LLM's outputs. What could go wrong, and how do you make it trustworthy?
answer_markdown: The core risk is that an unvalidated judge is a confident-sounding random number generator, and its scores get treated as ground truth because they arrive as numbers. Make it trustworthy by validating it: hand-grade a sample of maybe 30 to 50 outputs yourself, run the judge on the same sample, and measure agreement — aim for around 80 percent or better before trusting it, and tighten the rubric if you fall short. Beyond validation, three known biases need managing. Judges show position bias, favouring whichever answer appears first when comparing two, so randomise the order and ideally run both orderings. They show self-preference, rating text from their own model family more highly, which argues for using a different model as the judge than the one being graded. And they drift when the provider updates the model, so a score change may reflect your judge changing rather than your system — pin versions where possible and periodically re-validate. Run the judge at temperature 0 with a rubric that defines each score level concretely, since a vague rubric produces scores that wobble more than the real differences you are trying to detect.

prompt: Your RAG system's answer quality dropped after a release, but retrieval metrics are unchanged. Where do you look?
answer_markdown: The fact that you can ask this question is the point — measuring retrieval and generation separately is exactly what lets you eliminate half the system in one step. With recall at k unchanged, the correct chunks are still being retrieved and ranked, so the problem is downstream in generation. Look at what changed there: the generation prompt, the number of chunks being passed to the model, the model version if the provider updated it underneath you, and sampling parameters like temperature. A common specific cause is a change in how many chunks get passed — increasing from 5 to 15 raises the chance the answer is buried among distractors, and models measurably degrade at finding relevant information in a long context. Also check whether the context assembly order changed, since position within the prompt affects how reliably information is used. If nothing in your release explains it, compare outputs on the same golden cases before and after to characterise how the answers changed, which usually points directly at the cause.

prompt: What is the difference between offline and online evaluation, and why do you need both?
answer_markdown: Offline evaluation runs your golden dataset in CI before shipping: fast, repeatable, cheap, and it gates merges by catching regressions on cases you already know matter. Online evaluation measures real production traffic after shipping — thumbs-up rate, retry rate, escalation-to-human rate, task completion rate, conversation length. You need both because they catch fundamentally different things. Offline catches known regressions, which is most of what breaks, but it can only test cases someone thought to include, so it is blind to the inputs users actually send that nobody anticipated. Online catches those unknown unknowns and also catches drift, where quality degrades gradually because user behaviour shifted or the provider updated the model, neither of which shows up in a fixed test set. The healthy loop between them is that online failures become new offline cases: every production issue you diagnose gets added to the golden set so it can never regress silently again.

prompt: Your overall eval score stayed at 87% after a prompt change, so you shipped it. Users complained. What did you miss?
answer_markdown: Almost certainly a per-category regression hidden by the average. A single aggregate number can stay flat while one slice collapses — if billing questions dropped from 92% to 45% and technical questions rose from 82% to 95%, the mean barely moves while the experience for a whole class of users falls apart. Report scores per category and block on any category dropping beyond a threshold, rather than gating on the overall mean. Two related things to check: whether the categories in your golden set are weighted the way real traffic is, since a category that is 5% of your test set but 40% of production traffic will be badly under-represented in the average; and whether the failures cluster on cases that matter disproportionately, such as anything touching payments or account access, which deserve their own gate regardless of volume. The general principle is that an average is a summary and summaries hide exactly the distributional shifts you most need to see, so evaluation reports should show the breakdown by default and the aggregate as a secondary number.
